description: Reservation poverty, boarding schools and the Indian Citizenship Act 1924 — the 1920s boom passed Native Americans by.
content_html:
The Legacy of the Reservation System

By 1910, the fate of Native American peoples had already been largely determined by a century of displacement and conquest. The reservation system had forced the majority of Native Americans onto parcels of land that were often arid, economically marginal and isolated from markets and services. Tribes had been stripped of vast territories through a combination of military force, broken treaties and legal manipulation. The buffalo herds that had sustained Plains cultures had been deliberately hunted to near-extinction in the 1870s and 1880s.

Into this already diminished world, the Dawes Act of 1887 brought further devastation. The law broke up communally held tribal land into individual allotments — 160 acres per family — and sold the “surplus” land to white settlers. Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres of their remaining land — about two-thirds of what they had held in 1887. The allotment system destroyed the communal economic and social structures on which tribal life depended, without providing meaningful support for individual farming.

Key Fact

The Dawes Act of 1887 broke up communal tribal lands into individual allotments and sold the remaining land to white settlers. Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres — roughly two-thirds of their 1887 land holdings. By 1910, most reservations were poverty-stricken, with inadequate schools, healthcare and economic opportunities.

Native American Boarding Schools

The US government’s official policy towards Native Americans in this period was forced assimilation. The most direct tool of assimilation was the Native American boarding school system. The most famous was the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, founded in 1879. The philosophy behind these schools was summed up in the school’s founder Richard Henry Pratt’s phrase: “Kill the Indian, save the man.”

Children were taken from their families — sometimes by force — and transported to schools hundreds of miles away. At school they were forbidden to speak their native languages, wear traditional clothing or practise their religions. Their hair was cut. They were given English names. Punishments for speaking native languages could be severe. Death rates in boarding schools were high, partly from disease in crowded conditions, partly from inadequate care. By the early twentieth century, thousands of Native American children were passing through this system each year.

The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) was responsible for administering reservations and the boarding school system. Throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the BIA was plagued by corruption and incompetence. Agents who managed reservations often enriched themselves at the expense of the tribes they were supposed to serve. Food, medicine and resources allocated to reservations were frequently siphoned off. Congress periodically investigated scandals but effective reform was slow to materialise.

The 1928 Meriam Report, commissioned by the government, documented the catastrophic conditions on reservations in detail: extreme poverty, malnutrition, high disease rates, inadequate schools, and the failures of the Dawes allotment system. Its findings eventually contributed to the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 under President Franklin Roosevelt, which reversed the allotment policy. But through the 1910s and 1920s, conditions remained dire.

Key Fact

The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States. This was partly in recognition of the 12,000 Native Americans who had served in the US military during the First World War. However, citizenship did not automatically give Native Americans the right to vote in all states — several states maintained laws blocking them from voting well into the 1940s and beyond.

The Indian Citizenship Act, 1924

In 1924, Congress passed the Indian Citizenship Act, granting US citizenship to all Native Americans born within the borders of the United States. It was a significant symbolic recognition, partly prompted by the service of approximately 12,000 Native Americans in the First World War, many of them volunteers. Some Native Americans and their advocates welcomed it as a step towards equal rights. Others were deeply ambivalent: citizenship had not been asked for, came with conditions that undermined tribal sovereignty, and in several states did not translate into the right to vote.

While Wall Street boomed and flappers danced, conditions on most reservations barely changed. The majority of Native Americans lived in deep poverty, with life expectancy significantly below the national average. Unemployment on reservations was chronic. Access to healthcare and education was minimal by national standards. The federal government’s assimilation policy had failed on its own terms — it had destroyed traditional economies without successfully integrating Native Americans into the mainstream economy. The 1920s boom is a particularly stark illustration of the “nation of contrasts” theme: the most prosperous decade in American history to that point was, for Native Americans, simply another decade of dispossession and neglect.
exam_tip_html: The treatment of Native Americans is often overlooked in revision but is explicitly in the specification and may appear as part of a ‘nation of contrasts’ essay question. Make sure you can give specific evidence: the Dawes Act (1887) losing 90 million acres, the boarding school system and its assimilation policy, the Indian Citizenship Act (1924) and its limitations. For significance questions, contrast the symbolic importance of the 1924 Act with the continuing poverty on reservations and the voting restrictions that persisted in several states. This contrast illustrates perfectly why examiners reward top-band responses that weigh significance at the time against significance over time.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Dawes Act of 1887 broke up communal tribal lands, causing Native Americans to lose approximately 90 million acres by 1934. Reservations were characterised by poverty, inadequate healthcare and minimal economic opportunities throughout the 1910s and 1920s.
  • The government’s forced assimilation policy was implemented through Native American boarding schools that separated children from their families, banned native languages and suppressed traditional cultures. The Bureau of Indian Affairs administered reservations with chronic corruption and neglect.
  • The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 granted all Native Americans US citizenship, partly in recognition of 12,000 who had served in the First World War. However, several states continued to block Native Americans from voting, and reservation poverty continued unchanged through the boom years.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the reservation system in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Reservations confined Native Americans to areas of often poor-quality land far from their traditional territories [1], following the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and subsequent treaties which stripped tribes of their original lands. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Native American boarding school system.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature.
Feature 1: Children were removed from their families, sometimes by force, and forbidden to speak their native languages or practise their religions [1] — punishments for breaking these rules could be severe, and the philosophy was explicit in the motto 'Kill the Indian, save the man.' [1]
Feature 2: Death rates in boarding schools were high due to disease in crowded conditions and inadequate care [1] — thousands of Native American children passed through the system annually by the early twentieth century. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Dawes Act of 1887 harmed Native American communities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear causal chain from the Act's provisions to the harm caused, with specific evidence.
Secure: Valid explanation with supporting detail.
Developing: Names the Dawes Act but mechanism poorly explained.
Emerging: Simple point.
The Act broke up communally held tribal land into individual allotments and sold the 'surplus' to white settlers — between 1887 and 1934 Native Americans lost approximately 90 million acres. The destruction of communal land ownership eliminated the economic and social structures tribal life depended on, while the individual allotments of 160 acres were too small and often unsuitable for successful farming.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 for Native Americans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence; clear causal link from the Act to the outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: formal recognition of Native Americans as citizens for the first time; symbolic acknowledgement of military service in WWI; some Native Americans welcomed it as a step to equality; others saw it as undermining tribal sovereignty; practical limitation — several states still blocked Native Americans from voting into the 1940s.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 in improving the lives of Native Americans?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time; weighs the symbolic value against practical limitations; precise evidence.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may not distinguish between symbolic and practical significance.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: granted citizenship to all Native Americans born in the US; partly recognised 12,000 Native American First World War veterans; did not automatically grant voting rights — several states maintained restrictions.
Over time: laid symbolic groundwork for later civil rights recognition; however, reservation poverty, inadequate healthcare and education continued unchanged through the 1920s boom; the 1928 Meriam Report documented catastrophic conditions; real change came only with the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

practice_questions.text:
'The 1920s economic boom showed that America truly was a nation of contrasts.'
Using the treatment of Native Americans as evidence, how far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees using Native American experience alongside broader 1920s evidence; substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Simple agreement.
Agreement: while Wall Street boomed, Native Americans lived in chronic poverty on reservations; 90 million acres lost since Dawes Act; boarding schools deliberately destroyed culture; BIA corruption and neglect documented; voting rights withheld in several states even after 1924; 1928 Meriam Report confirmed catastrophic conditions.
Disagreement (limits of the contrast argument): the 1920s boom was also unequal for farmers, Black Americans and recent immigrants — Native Americans were not uniquely excluded; the 1924 Act was at least a step.
Judgement: Native American experience is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that the boom was built on deep inequality — the 'nation of contrasts' thesis holds strongly here.

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Dawes Act of 1887 do to Native American land?
options: It extended reservation boundaries to include more fertile land
It broke up communally held tribal land into individual allotments and sold the surplus to white settlers
It returned tribal land that had been illegally seized
It created a new system of communal farming on reservations

knowledge_checks.q: What did the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 grant?
options: The right to vote in all states
The return of reservation land taken under the Dawes Act
US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States
The closure of Native American boarding schools

knowledge_checks.q: Between 1887 and 1934, Native Americans lost approximately _____ million acres of land as a result of the Dawes Act's allotment system.
The government agency responsible for administering reservations and the boarding school system was the _____ of Indian Affairs.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: 1924 law granting US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States
1887 law that broke up communal tribal lands into individual allotments
Policy of erasing Native American culture to absorb people into mainstream society

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Dawes Act of 1887 do?
flashcard_questions.a: It broke up communal tribal land into individual allotments of 160 acres and sold the surplus to white settlers.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how much land did Native Americans lose between 1887 and 1934 as a result of the Dawes Act?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 90 million acres — about two-thirds of their 1887 land holdings.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the philosophy behind Native American boarding schools?
flashcard_questions.a: Forced assimilation — to destroy Native culture and language while teaching English and Christianity.

flashcard_questions.q: Who founded the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania in 1879?
What was the Bureau of Indian Affairs and what was its reputation?
flashcard_questions.a: The federal agency administering reservations; notorious for corruption and neglect throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 grant to Native Americans?
flashcard_questions.a: US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the United States.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924 passed, partly?
flashcard_questions.a: In recognition of the approximately 12,000 Native Americans who had served in the US military during the First World War.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the 1928 Meriam Report document about reservation conditions?
flashcard_questions.a: Extreme poverty, malnutrition, high disease rates, inadequate schools, and the failures of the Dawes allotment system.

flashcard_questions.q: What practical limitation meant the Indian Citizenship Act did not give all Native Americans equal political rights?
flashcard_questions.a: Several states maintained laws blocking Native Americans from voting, well into the 1940s and beyond.

glossary_terms.definition: Areas of land set aside by the US government for Native American peoples to live on, following the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and subsequent treaties, typically on poor-quality land removed from traditional territories.

A US law passed in 1887 that broke up communally held tribal lands into individual plots of 160 acres per family, with the aim of turning Native Americans into individual farmers and assimilating them into American society.
The deliberate process of erasing Native American culture, language and identity in order to absorb Native people into mainstream white American society.

Residential schools, funded by the US government and often run by churches, that removed Native American children from their families and communities to educate them in English and Christian values while suppressing their native languages and cultures.

The federal government agency responsible for managing relations between the US government and Native American tribes, founded in 1824, notorious for corruption and neglect throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
A US law passed in 1924 that granted citizenship to all Native Americans born within the borders of the United States, partly in recognition of their military service in the First World War.
A 1928 government-commissioned investigation that documented catastrophic conditions on Native American reservations, including extreme poverty, malnutrition and inadequate healthcare and education.
